title: Ancient DNA Links Ice Age Europeans Across the Continent
paragraphs: A study in the journal Science Advances has used ancient DNA to look at life in Europe during the Ice Age. The research was led by the University of Vienna, and 37 scientists took part. It focuses on the Gravettian culture, which lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.

The most important result comes from a woman who lived about 30,000 years ago in Isturitz Cave, in France. Her genome is the oldest of its kind from southwestern Europe. Most of her ancestry was western European, but she also carried ancestry from central and eastern Europe. The team estimates that groups from east and west mixed between about 32,500 and 31,500 years ago. One of the researchers, Pere Gelabert, said that the two populations “were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed.”

The team also recovered DNA from the soil of El Mirón Cave in Spain, from a layer about 22,000 years old, although no human bones were found there. This suggests that western ancestry survived the coldest period of the Ice Age in that region. However, the main finding rests on one woman, so more genomes are needed to confirm the picture.
